newsitem.title: UK: Hong Kong credit rating reaffirmed.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong credit rating reaffirmed.

text.p: Hong Kong's A plus long-term foreign currency rating was reaffirmed on Thursday by European credit rating agency IBCA, only seven months before the British colony is due to be handed over to Chinese rule.

IBCA said it believed China would honour the Basic Law and Joint Declaration and consequently Hong Kong would retain all the economic attributes of a separate state and continue to perform most impressively.

"The 'One country, two systems' formula allows some flexibility for varying interpretations and there were always going to be occasional alarms and accusations of bad faith by some," the IBCA statement said.

"By and large, however, it is IBCA's view that the Chinese Government will continue to be bound by its word in line with its own...interests, including Hong Kong's strengths as a port, financial centre and source of foreign direct investment."
IBCA said the A plus rating applied to senior and unsecured sovereign debt issues and set a ceiling for all other Hong Kong issuers.

IBCA also affirmed its rating of A1 plus for short-term issues and has for the first time issued a rating of AA plus for sovereign issues in Hong Kong dollars. It said it would again set a ceiling for all other debt issuers in local currency.

"The gap between IBCA's A plus rating and the AA plus, even AAA, rating which Hong Kong might expect on economic factors alone reflects the remaining doubt concerning China's ultimate ability to deliver as intended," the statement said.
"It would take a massive upheaval in China to deflect the leadership from a policy which has now been followed for many years," it continued.
IBCA said the economic policies of the Hong Kong government had not wavered as transition to Chinese rule approached.

They remained enviably cautious and successful, permitting the territory to transform itself with relatively little difficulty into an advanced services economy, while relocating the bulk of its former manufacturing economy into the neighbouring low cost provinces of China.
